A Necessary Conjunction: Dockar-Drysdale and Winnicott

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves

UK
e-mail: reeves.gorseacre@btinternet.com

Christopher Reeves   Retired child psychotherapist. He first met Barbara Dockar-Drysdale while a psychology undergraduate at Oxford in 1962. Following his psychotherapy training he practised as a child psychotherapist in Hertfordshire, before succeeding Mrs Dockar-Drysdale as Therapeutic Adviser to the Mulberry Bush School in 1975, subsequently becoming Principal there from 1981 to 1991.
Winnicott, Dockar-Drysdale, Mulberry Bush School, therapeutic education,

This paper examines the professional relationship and mutual influence of Winnicott and Dockar-Drysdale, particularly in relation to the development of the therapeutic principles underlying the treatment philosophy of the Mulberry Bush School. The first half of the paper considers evolving notions of therapeutic need and the provision of opportunities of regressive experience for unintegrated children in a residential setting. The second half considers the implications of this provision in the thinking of both, in terms of the organizational structure, staff consultation and demands of and on the support network.

Learning from Reading: Henry James's Novel What Maisie Knew

Graham Shulman

Graham Shulman

110 Main Street

Graham Shulman   Child and adolescent psychotherapist who trained at the Tavistock Clinic. He is Senior Tutor for the clinical child psychotherapy training at the Scottish Institute of Human Relations, where he also teaches on other courses. In addition to his interests in clinical work and teaching, he has an interest in literature and the relationship between literature and psychoanalysis.
Knowledge; Oedipal situation; omniscience; narrative; reading; metaphor.

This paper discusses a central theme of the novel What Maisie Knew by Henry James, namely the development of a child's consciousness and internal world in a hostile psychological environment. It explores the way in which the novel dramatizes the problems for a child, in such circumstances, of knowing and understanding her own experience and the adult world. The paper charts the difficulties for Maisie in negotiating a child's ordinary tasks and stages of psychic growth, and in particular the Oedipal situation. It also explores the parallel in the novel between the child's attempts to know and the attempts of the reader of fiction to know, and the use of reading as a metaphor for perception and learning.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Aul Barrows and Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham  

This issue contains a range of papers of clinical, theoretical and historical interest, reflecting both the breadth of work undertaken by child psychotherapists and the consolidation and development of theoretical concepts based on accumulated clinical experience.

Reeves’ paper traces the mutual influence of Winnicott and Docker-Drysdale on each other in the area of work with deprived children. The paper arises out of Reeves’ long involvement with the Mulberry Bush School and reflects his familiarity with, and depth of knowledge of, the work of both these clinicians. It is a paper that will be of interest to the many child psychotherapists involved in consulting to children's homes or other forms of residential provision, and brings to attention the important work pioneered by Dockar-Drysdale in this area.

Miller's paper, like the subsequent ones on autism, builds upon the work done by child psychotherapists with patient groups once considered unsuitable for treatment. This paper, like Pecotic's, considers the child's response to what he or she sees in the eyes of the mother and the feelings that are reflected in them. Both believe that what the baby encounters there - be it the disappointment Miller describes or the ‘black hole’ found by Pecotic's patient - is crucial to the development of the self, the capacity for relating, the development of the mind and the ability to think. This way of conceptualizing experience is presumably a reflection of the centrality of infant observation in the training of child psychotherapists. Both papers also underline the particular necessity for careful examination of transference/countertransference experiences in order to reach conclusions about the nature of early object relations and how these get re-evoked in the therapist-patient relationship.

In this edition there are three papers concerned with children on the autistic spectrum. These papers seek to further the conceptualization of these mental states, pioneered by child psychotherapists and often reported in this journal, and the technical modifications that so often seem necessary, flowing out of these theoretical developments.

Two Way Street: Communicating with Disabled Children and Young PeopleTraining Video and Handbook NSPCC Joseph Rowntree Foundation & Triangle, 2001

John Woods

John Woods

Respond
3rd floor, 24-32 Stephenson Way
London NWI 2HD

John Woods  

This video and accompanying handbook make an excellent introduction to the requirements of communicating with young people with learning disability. Running for twenty-five minutes, and along with the suggested exercises, it represents a very significant advance in the awareness of the needs of this particular group of young people. As well as an effective statement of the need for better communication, there are concise descriptions of the various methods that have been developed, from sign language to the individually tailored system for people with specific disabilities. The title was provided by Holly Williams, herself a young woman with learning difficulties, who was one of the ‘video core group’.

The project drew from several special schools in the Brighton area and has an aura of authenticity, because it involved a ‘consultative’ group of young people. As the handbook explains, the starting point is that, despite the good intentions of several government reports, there is still a lamentable lack of awareness about the need for young people with learning difficulties to be communicated with over many aspects of their lives. ‘Does he take sugar?’ is unfortunately still alive and kicking. The video goes on with the depiction of stereotypes of learning disability, which, portrayed as they are by those very people, makes uncomfortable viewing. As they themselves go on to describe their ‘bad experiences with professionals’, I was reminded of how we workers in the field have to overcome our own sense of inability to communicate with someone who has special needs. We are given advice in this programme, to ‘keep calm’, ‘don't be afraid to make mistakes’, ‘don't be scared to ask if you don't understand’, ‘show an interest in us, make it more than just a job’.

The commitment of these young people to communicate with each other as well as with their audience is very moving. I was reminded of my own difficulty, acute at first, and still occasionally so, when, feeling bereft of my usual communication skills, I begin to really know what it is to feel isolated and misunderstood. The handbook warns of the emotional impact that this video may have on a training group, and very sensibly advises paying careful attention not only to the reactions of the group but also to the trainers’ own aims and objectives.

Editorial

Paul Barrows and Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham  

We are very pleased that this issue contains three papers from overseas, reflecting the truly international nature of the journal. There are two contributions from Italy and one from France.

The first two papers continue themes from recent editions, illustrating the current interests of child psychotherapists in the applications of psychotherapy outside clinic settings and in work with autistic children. Diana Cant's paper is about her work with children living in a therapeutic community. It picks up some of the themes written about in recent papers in this journal by Reeves (28/1) and Sprince (28/2). It will be of interest to the many child psychotherapists working with this client population of highly deprived children in the care system; also to the large number of child psychotherapists involved in consulting to children's homes, residential units and therapeutic communities. Cant's paper looks at the role of the child psychotherapist in providing treatment within a therapeutic community as part of the overall package of care and treatment the child receives. It therefore raises interesting and complicated questions in relation to technique and the boundaries of sessions. Morra's paper considers the connection between child psychosis and autism and looks at the thorny problem of notions of fixation and regression in relation to the aetiology and structure of these disorders.

The paper by Case and the jointly authored paper by Bertolini and Nissim approach the concept of the child's imagination and how this develops or is impaired. Both papers argue for the need in some children for imagination to grow in a space somewhat removed from the therapy room. With Case's patient, such a moment of development happens while looking out of the therapy room window, whereas with Bertolini's and Nissim's patients imagination develops in the virtual space of video games. Persuasive arguments are put forward in both papers that a distant way of relating can be a prelude to more intimate engagement with the therapist and to a type of playing more rooted in the exploration of the interface between internal and external realities.

Psychotherapy of an Adolescent Presenting a Mystical Delusion

An Illustration of Splitting Processes and Their Consequences

Albert Ciccone and David Alcorn

David Alcorn

40 Avenue Berthelot
38200 Vienne
France
albert.ciccone@univ-lyon2.fr

David Alcorn  

Splitting, narcissistic defences, reintegration of split-off parts, internal gang, claustrum,

The paper discusses the psychotherapy of an adolescent who, during a psychotic breakdown, developed a mystical delusion on a religious theme. Splitting processes and the narcissistic defences that accompany them are illustrated. After showing how the patient had recourse to splitting and how the split-off parts of the ego took refuge inside an internal object, the ego's efforts to make contact once more with these split-off aspects and to reintegrate them are highlighted. With the help of certain concepts developed by, for example, Rosenfeld and Meltzer — specifically those relating to the organization of internal groupings or ‘gangs’ and their destructiveness and the compartmentalization of internal objects — the author shows how certain particularities of the patient's internal world can be understood in terms of these splitting processes. In addition the clinical material presented raises several technical questions, in particular those relating to dissociative processes and delusion or delusional theories as they become manifest in the treatment.

Evanthe Blandy  

The theory of psychoanalysis has come to be applied to a large number of treatment modalities since the Second World War. In the introduction to his book, Untying the Knot: Working with Children and Parents, Dr Brafman makes a case for revisiting Donald Winnicott's ideas about the ‘therapeutic intervention’ (1971). He states that his aim is to set out a clinical approach to cases where the referred patient is a child or adolescent, but where the parents are intimately involved in the consultation.

In the second chapter, ‘The clinical encounter’, Brafman considers various issues which arise in the clinical encounter. One has a sense of someone chatting about his work in a relaxed collegiate manner. He is humorous, giving technical tips about how to put children and parents at their ease to get things going: for example, after listening to the child, he turns to the parents and says ‘And who are you?’ This chapter prepares the way for the following three chapters, which give clinical accounts of eleven children aged 13 months to 15 years with varying degrees of parental interaction.

The focus in the initial contact is not to discover the ‘correct facts’, but how the child interprets what is going on around him. His priority is to engage the child in a joint venture to discover the unconscious fantasy or conflict underlying the presenting symptom. The symptom, whether it is headaches, enuresis, constipation or more overtly psychological problems, such as anxieties, phobias or nightmares, may already have received attention from other health professionals to little avail. By the time the child reaches the psychoanalytic consultant, Dr Brafman, he is ready to ‘find’ an object he can communicate with. The consultant occupies the place of the child's ‘subjective object’, as if the child already ‘knows’ him. The encounter with the consultant therefore offers a precious opportunity which can be seized, and something ‘magical’ transpires when the child feels his communication has been understood. Winnicott calls this potential meeting a ‘sacred moment’, which can either be used or wasted.

Emanuel Lewis  

The ten authors know each other's way of working and have been associated with the Tavistock Marital Studies Institute, the Tavistock Clinic and the British Psycho-Analytical Society. A partial exception is Ruth Skrine, a retired GP who has been chairman of the Institute of Psychosexual Medicine. To make best use of this book requires a working knowledge of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. A shared psychotherapeutic focus is a close attention to the patient's emotional relationship with the therapists and the therapist's emotional response to their patients. This transference-countertransference of thoughts and feelings is taken as being present from the beginning of the encounter. To be emotionally involved with the patient while at the same time observing and reflecting with a part of our mind, taking up a ‘third position’ (Britton, 1989), helps understand the nature of the marriage. This reflection continues after the sessions when we try to understand our own unconscious thoughts and feelings. The exposition is not just dry theory as all the chapters present vivid and instructive clinical descriptions which illustrate how the therapy is applied to make sense of a marriage and to convey this understanding to patients.

As the authors use similar psychoanalytic theories in their writing there is an inherent consistency and an agreeable absence of contentious argument in the book, unusual in a multi-author book.

The main aim of the book is to describe, discuss and evaluate brief marital treatment in various settings. The reviewer enjoyed this excellent book and can recommend it to all who work, or intend to work, with couples, especially in time-limited settings. The editor provides a detailed introduction. To anyone with access to his introduction this review is superfluous.

In Chapter 1, Mary Morgan focuses on initial consultations and suggests that the therapist couple needs to hold a ‘couple state of mind’, and she links this idea with the capacity to take a ‘third position’, which can not only facilitate the diagnostic formulation but help to contain the patient's anxiety. This containment may help anxious and angry patients decide to accept ongoing treatment. As with all the chapters, the theory is enlivened by clinical illustrations.

Peter Evans  

The British researcher into masculinity construction Mairtin Mac an Ghaill (1994) recounts a telling incident from his years as a secondary school teacher. An adolescent boy had shown his gratitude to Mac an Ghaill for helping him pass an exam by giving him a bunch of flowers in the playground. There was much macho humour among the teachers in the staff room afterwards. Later in the day the same boy was involved in a fight with some other boys, who attacked him for being ‘gay’ because of the flower-giving incident. In the aftermath of the fight, Mac an Ghaill was summoned to the office of the Head, who had let it be known that he thought that Mac an Ghaill had ‘really gone too far this time’. Anticipating some form of interrogation-cum-dressing down over the fight, Mac an Ghaill was preparing to protest that he could not be held responsible for the fight. In fact, he was surprised to find that the fight was not what was bothering the Head at all. On the contrary, the Head had been rattled by untoward behaviour of an altogether different sort: the unmanly gesture of a boy giving a male teacher a bunch of flowers. Broken noses and black eyes paled into insignificance compared with this form of transgression.

One of the most compelling findings generated by this painstaking and sensitive study by Frosh, Phoenix and Pattman is that pervasive homophobia sets serious limits on the forms of masculinity constructed and lived out by young secondary-school-aged boys. The study is both illuminating and potently generative of fresh thinking about masculine identity construction in young adolescents. It is also moving and urgent at both therapeutic and social policy levels.

The research project aimed to explore emerging masculinities in the early teenage years. Two-hundred and forty-five boys and twenty-seven girls between the ages of 11 and 14 years were interviewed, drawn from twelve secondary schools in London (four from the private or ‘independent’ sector and eight from the state sector, of which four were boys’ schools and eight co-educational). Group interviews (of between four and six young people) were initially conducted, most of them with boys in single-sex groups but some with mixed groups of boys and girls talking together about boys. Some of the boys who had taken part in the original group interview were invited to take part in two follow-up individual interviews, spaced apart by two weeks. The interviews with boys, both group and individual, were conducted with exemplary restraint and sensitivity by Rob Pattman, adopting a ‘clinical style’ which allowed the participants to speak as freely as possible on the issues raised. The follow-up individual interviews explored repetitions, contradictions and gaps in the material from the first (group) interview.

When Autistic Isn't Necessarily Autism

Cathy Urwin

Cathy Urwin

Flat 1 18 Alexandra Grove London N4 2LF, UK
e-mail: cathy.urwin@ukgateway.net

Cathy Urwin   Child and adult psychotherapist working in the NHS in East London and in private practice. She has a background in developmental psychology and has published research on early social interaction and language development in sighted and non-sighted children. She is particularly interested in work with under-5s and is currently involved in a local Sure Start initiative.
Autistic spectrum; language development; language delay; multicultural; trauma.

This paper describes family work with four children from different ethnic backgrounds presenting with autistic features in the context of delayed or deviant language development and, in one case, elective mutism. It begins by describing how psychoanalytic approaches to language development have tended to see the process as underpinned by symbol formation as a compensation for loss of the object. This is contrasted with an approach which, following Bion, emphasizes language development as an aspect of a broad process concerned with enabling emotional experience to become thought. I also emphasize the significance of the survival and development of the self in achieving separation. In the case studies, the paper highlights the degree of trauma in the parents' backgrounds, which had impeded them from containing their children's developmental anxieties. The parents' telling their stories was both valuable to them and enabled them to become more emotionally available to their children. In all cases the work promoted language development and autistic features disappeared or waned considerably after relatively brief intervention. The conclusions discuss the relevance of these findings to the autistic child population, and the value of child psychotherapy to differential diagnosis within the autistic spectrum.

Editorial

Paul Barrows and Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham

Hamish Canham  

While the core work of the child psychotherapist remains the practice of individual psychoanalytic psychotherapy, the numbers of children who can be helped in this way must remain relatively limited. It is, in part, in recognition of this constraint that child psychotherapists have sought to apply psychoanalytic insights in various contexts beyond the consulting room.

The collection of papers gathered in this Special Edition on Applied Work bears witness to the fruits of that enterprise and demonstrates its value. The paper by Canham applies a psychoanalytic paradigm to group work with children with particular reference to the work of Rosenfeld. There has been a long tradition of such group work in the profession, often based in primary schools, though it has been relatively little written about (see, however, Reid, 1999). Canham's paper demonstrates the value of this approach and implicit in his account is the sense that group work is not simply a means of increasing the number of children who can be seen at any one time but rather, has its own very particular value. Perhaps this should not be surprising since it is often the child's difficulty in managing within a group setting that prompts their referral.

The following three papers, in a sense, pursue this theme of ‘groups’ and ‘gangs’. Jackson moves on to consider the wider ‘group’ in which children function, namely the school, while Sprince describes her work in a therapeutic community where it is the explicit function of the ‘group’ to be the agent of therapy. Emanuel, on the other hand, describes a project in which initially the focus was on the provision of individual therapy to children in care, but where it rapidly became apparent that this made little sense without addressing the dynamics of the larger, organizational ‘group’ in which those children found themselves. All three authors chose to work indirectly through providing consultation to the staff, and the main theme to emerge from each paper is the centrality of the workers’ countertransference experiences. When these feelings can be openly addressed, and thought given to the extent to which they represent communications about the experiences of the children or clients, then a major shift takes place. Acting out is replaced by reflection and more appropriate responses. In each case we can see how the containing function of the consultant to the group has facilitated the emergence of a ‘group state of mind’, allowing the group to learn from their own experiences in a mature and thoughtful way. It is impressive work.

This book attempts a ‘fresh approach’ to Melanie Klein's work, ‘offering an exploration of the themes that gradually gain momentum in her early papers and placing these in the broader context of professional debates which spurred her thinking’ (p. 5). This is an important aim, and the book is a serious contribution to Klein studies. After Klein's death there was a concerted attempt by her followers to make her work accessible through didactic books and articles (e.g. Segal, 1964, 1979). However latterly, in the last ten years or more, there has been an attempt at a more reflective approach to her ideas and practice (Petot, 1990; Spillius, 1988; Hinshelwood, 1989) with works that do not demand allegiance, and avoid prejudicial dismissal - pitfalls which many secondary sources tend to fall into. Likierman's book falls into this category of reflective study of Klein, and it is an important evaluation of Klein's work and historical position. It is not intended as a didactic text informing students of Melanie Klein's thinking although much can be gained from reading it as an educational text. In fact it is more of a work of history, a conceptual history of one strand of psychoanalytic thinking from around 1926 to 1960.

It is not a clinical work nor does it make reference to later Kleinian thinking. It is in fact a close reading of Klein's own papers. Approximately half the book concerns the context for Klein's early work and papers, prior to the depressive position in 1935. Likierman's ‘fresh approach’ to this oeuvre is certainly written with a freshness of style. It covers the significant conceptual contributions which Klein introduced into British psychoanalysis excellently. The first half of the book largely deals with context and the formative influences on her, especially that of Ferenczi. The second half the well-known theoretical developments of the depressive position, paranoid-schizoid position and primary envy; and with equal excellence it points up and debates a number of problematic issues, some of them original and important.

In recent publications about autism, psychoanalysis is barely mentioned and is often seen as outdated. In particular, psychoanalysis is accused of putting additional blame on mothers, who are already suffering enough, and of offering nothing but expensive therapies that amount to little in the end. They claim latest research to have shown that autism is basically a complicated neurological rather than a psychodynamic disorder. The name that is often associated with a psychoanalytic approach to dealing with autism is that of Bruno Bettelheim: what is not mentioned is that Bettelheim was the first ever actually to attempt a systematic residential therapy of autistic children. However, his concept of establishing a friendly and supportive therapeutic environment tailored entirely to the needs of the children is, in fact, exactly the same as those therapies and training programmes that want nothing to do with psychoanalysis, and thus have no idea what they owe to it.

There is also never any mention (presumably because it is not even noticed) that psychoanalysts have continued their work following the publication of Bettelheim's last monograph on the treatment of autistic children in 1967. Very different theories and concepts of treatment have been developed, illustrated with detailed case studies. Let me mention only Margaret Mahler, Francis Tustin, Esther Bick, Donald Meltzer, Thomas Ogden, Anne Alvarez, Maria Rhode from the English-speaking world, and Maud Mannoni, Rosine and Robert Lefort, Geneviève Haag, Piera Aulagnier and Marie-Christine Laznik-Penot from France. The list could go on. Psychoanalysis is not criticized by modern autism research, which would be legitimate and useful, it is simply ignored. This is not only wrong, but it also does not help autistic children.

Sybille Janert does not directly address this division of opinion, and she is right not to do so, because, if she had, her book would have been unlikely to attract many readers.

A computer hacker who was eventually caught, used to sign himself online as ‘Erik Weisz’. It turned out that he had chosen as pseudonym the real name of a late nineteenth-century magician and escape artist - the famous Houdini. In a sense, hackers are the cyber Houdinis of today, albeit that they devise ever more ingenious ways of getting into rather than out of impossible places. Like the original Houdini, they are attracted by increasingly elaborate obstacles and by the constant threat of detection. The state of mind that seeks such challenges, along with Houdini's life and psyche, are some of the topics explored in this insightful book.

The book begins with a situation that is familiar - at least to child psychotherapists. Phillips is in the therapy room with a little girl who insists on a strange and frustrating opening ritual to her sessions: she stands in the middle of the room, shuts her eyes tightly, claims that she is hiding and demands to be found. Whatever the therapist's response, she is not satisfied. Phillips notes that what he has found already, which is ‘her in the middle of the room, hiding - is obviously not what she wants me to look for’. The girl, eyes still shut, says urgently that she cannot escape, and is trapped. The therapist is under an even greater pressure to ‘find’ and release her. Phillips realizes that she has created a therapeutic entrapment, because her ritual never changes and because ‘what I say - even though it is as different as I can make it each time, even though I rack my brains for what she wants to hear - seems equally repetitious’. Furthermore, according to her parents, this game is repeated with friends until they tire of it. Everyone becomes impatient with her, and, Phillips suggests, impatience is ‘something that always verges on indifference’.

As child psychotherapists we experience countless such moments of enigma and frustration in our working lives. They push us to act out, to become impatient and indifferent instead of staying with the frustration and discovering how to think about it. We devote many hours to discussing technique that is precisely intended to prevent acting out in all its forms. But Phillips takes the subject further than a here-and-now technique issue. His little patient challenges his ability not only to contain frustration in the session, but also to ‘find’ her psychically. She also leads him to a broader consideration of issues of entrapment and escape in human psychical life, and Houdini is his excellent route into this study.

Branka Pecotic   Trained as a child and adolescent psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic and works at the Brent Child and Family Clinic, London. Earlier, she trained abroad as a clinical psychologist and adult psychoanalytic psychotherapist and has worked in that capacity at the Barnet, Enfield and Harringey MH NHS Trust. She teaches on postgraduate courses at the Tavistock Clinic and lectures at universities in the UK and abroad. She is a tutor and supervisor on child and adult psychoanalytic psychotherapy trainings in Belgrade. She runs psychotherapy groups with children, parents and adults and consults to organizations as part of her work in Brent.
Autism; black hole; maternal depression; internal objects.

The metaphor of the ‘black hole’ has been borrowed from astronomy in order to describe certain phenomena occurring in work with autistic and psychotic children. This metaphor is different from Tustin's concept of the ‘black hole’. I shall attempt to describe another phenomenon: not that of the hole in the self, resulting from premature separation, but the hole in the object that the autistic or psychotic child is relating to—or, rather, turning away from.

I describe an autistic boy's need to protect himself against the catastrophic experience of relating to an object with such a hole in its mind. That is a particular kind of a depressed object which emits deadness, instead of the lively, responsive affect that the child should get in communication. It is not an intrusive object, but it sucks in and drowns energy.

If the experience of relating to the ‘black hole’ in the object happens early and in such a powerful way that the child's energy feels insufficient to defend against it in any way, then the fear of annihilation becomes so strong that it may lead to the wiping out of the whole internal universe in order to escape its deadly gravitational pull. Only when a different kind of relationship gets internalized, through therapy, with an object that contains and returns life and energy, can the mind grow enough to be able to communicate the other, darker side of the relationship from which it has closed itself away.

Kathy Duguid  

This innovative book, based on eighty experiences of therapy with children and adolescents in care, should be read by all child psychotherapists. The introduction clearly describes the role of the child psychotherapist and the clinical setting, but the book will be of enormous interest and use to the whole range of professionals working with children in care and their carers.

The clinical experiences with children are sharply observed and described. Margaret Hunter is particularly skilled at naming and interpreting her countertransference in an open manner. The particular difficulties of connecting with children who have often had what seems like a lifetime of dealing with neglectful and abusing parental figures comes to life quickly in the text. There are evocative descriptions of extremely vulnerable children who have learnt to ‘wrong foot’ adults and leave the therapist not knowing what will contain and begin to make sense of their profound experiences of abandonment. One of the central themes of the book is that of emotional containment in the therapy sessions - the complex issues of when to ‘hold on’ to the child's projections and when to give them back as interpretations are explored in different clinical examples.

This book immediately challenges stereotyped ideas of technique and of when therapy is a possible treatment. Hunter emphasizes the need for flexibility and open mindedness in thinking about how child psychotherapy can contribute to the child in care. She ably demonstrates that children can be treated, with good effect, even when they are in transitional placements. She also describes the usefulness of the assessment process, providing that the child and the care network are clear about the rules of engagement and confidentiality.

Hunter recognizes how useful such an emotional snapshot can be for social work teams trying to fit services to the needs of accommodated children and she sensitively appreciates that social workers frequently have insufficient time or permission to get to know the child themselves. The psychoanalytic emphasis on internal identifications and the importance of emotional processes, Hunter shows, prove to be stable indications of a child's psychological traits.

Ezekiel; Klein; poet; prophet; superego.

The prophet Ezekiel had a seminal influence on later poets. This speculative paper explores the ways in which he may have chosen to experience disturbed states of mind in order to reintegrate parts of his psyche split off in infancy. It discusses his dialogues with his primitive superego (the agent of the original splitting) and the superego's subsequent metamorphosis. It also suggests that Ezekiel may have given us a poetic account of the experience of reintegration, as well as metaphors for the new levels of psychic maturity resulting from this process.

Staff dynamics; residential units; sexual abuse; organizational consultancy; multiply traumatized children.

This paper is a brief account of my work as consultant psychotherapist to various residential units for multiply traumatized and sexually abused adolescents. I attempt to describe the organizational structures that I have helped to put in place, and to give some description of how they have been used. I try to demonstrate how a staff group actively working on understanding themselves and their own process of relating can create a culture that encourages such children to respect this endeavour and engage in it themselves. I give some examples of how the learning in the adult group is mirrored in the children's group.

The paper explores, in detail, the process of a single assessment as it unfolds session by session. It draws attention to the inevitability of the clinician's harbouring preconceptions of all kinds — especially when working with adolescents. It focuses on the difficulty of withstanding those preconceptions and allowing the patient's true anxieties, conscious and unconscious, to emerge. The process is a complex one requiring close attention to transference and countertransference manifestations, to the central significance of observation, to Bion's notion of the opacity of memory and desire. The case, that of a hypochondriacal 17-year-old young woman, highlights some main concerns and defences of the age group, for example, somatization, separation, fears of madness, issues of identity and, most fundamental of all, sexuality.

This paper explores the meaning of video games from a psychotherapeutic perspective, addressing the technical problem of whether or not this type of play activity favours the development of the infantile transference. Clinical material drawn from intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy with two children forms the basis for description of the different meanings the video game may assume during the course of the therapeutic process. Particular attention will be paid to the countertransference experience and to the changes in the therapeutic attitude that are necessary in order to facilitate the use of the video game as a tool for communication. Paediatric liaison, psychosomatics, psychoanalytic psychiatry, psychiatric diagnosis,

Paediatric liaison work requires an appreciation of the interweaving of the different factors involved when a child has physical symptoms. Psychoanalytic psychotherapy is usually viewed simply as a potential treatment option. This paper argues that its use is both therapeutic and diagnostic and that it should be valued for this breadth of contribution. The therapeutic process is conducted in a way that can promote an understanding of the child and their context and thus enhance the ability to meet the child's needs by all involved in their care. This can be achieved without sacrificing the degree of privacy that the psychotherapist/patient relationship requires. Material is presented from the psychotherapy of a child who had an hereditary condition which moved unexpectedly into a terminal phase after psychotherapy was started. Examples are given to illustrate the importance of the understanding gained from therapy and how, through an integrative process, it was used to assist the overall care. The material also describes the potential diagnostic use of information from psychotherapy when this is formulated by consideration of conscious and unconscious mechanisms alongside mental state phenomenology. This has implications for the relationships between disciplines and for their training requirements.

Some of the literature connected with child psychosis and autism (Freud, Klein, Kanner, Segal, Stern, Tustin) is examined, together with different hypotheses about its psychological aetiology. Special attention is given to the problem of fixation/regression, which is quite controversial. An example is provided of a child, basically autistic, who can be seen as being in an intermediate state between a psychotic and an obsessional disorder. With this, another controversial problem arises: is there any similarity between the rituals of autism and those of obsessional neurosis? And what about the withdrawal of affects we find in both? A psychotherapy case is then presented, describing a child with significant autistic features, 9 years old at the beginning of the treatment. He has a twin brother, who presents with a rather confusional psychosis, in therapy with another therapist. My patient showed erratic contact, stereotypical behaviour, very little language and confused accounts of stories from television, film and cartoons. In the course of treatment a quasi-delusional state also appeared. Even though he was mute in the main, sometimes his attachment to me shown in the transference gave me the feeling of a baby in his first phases of emotional development. Surprisingly he showed some capacity to play with toys in a constructive way — a sign of limited improvement.

Further considerations are given in conclusion, dealing with the structure of childhood psychosis. Autism and confusional psychosis are considered as being basically one structure, with different pictures, easily interchangeable. Sometimes my patient's expressions, through either some elementary play or his rituals, seemed halfway between pre-symbolic and symbolic. Some features typical of the paranoid-schizoid position can be recognized: feelings of persecution, massive projective identification and fragmentation.

Caroline Case   Works as a child psychotherapist at Knowle Clinic, Bristol. She trained at the Scottish Institute of Human Relations in Edinburgh. She is also in private practice as an analytical art therapist. She is co-editor of Working with Children in Art Therapy (Routledge, 1990) and co-author of The Handbook of Art Therapy (Routledge, 1992). Severe deprivation, animation, aesthetic reciprocity, shared attention, framing of experience,

This paper discusses the development of animation and imaginative activity in a case in which there has been previous severe deprivation. Clinical material from work with an 8-year-old boy will illustrate how omnipotent behaviour, which has the function of keeping fear and feeling form consciousness, can give way to imaginative interaction with the environment. I suggest that, when internal objects have been frozen, it may be safer for the child to see animation outside the room. This may be a necessary stage before a child can begin to play with the therapist inside the room. I am using the term ‘animation’ in the sense of new imaginative play that has been stimulated by an apprehension of beauty in nature. This is contrasted with driven manic defending against awareness of self and others.

Deprivation, ‘looked-after children’, disorganized attachment, social services professionals, consultation,

The author describes her experience of setting up a therapeutic service for ‘looked-after children’ in a social services department, and the change of approach from a focus on individual therapy to consultation and liaison with the network. The idea that children in the ‘care system’ suffer a triple deprivation when the ‘double deprivation’, as described by Henry (1974), is compounded by organizational difficulties, is explored. Material is presented of work with foster-parents which helped to prevent placement breakdown. The ways in which disturbing emotional states of clients are re-enacted within the organization are discussed. The author suggests that the paralysis in a social services system, which can lead to ‘drift’, resembles the ‘collapse of strategy’ of babies displaying a ‘disorganized/disoriented’ attachment response to a frightened or frightening mother. The need for a ‘secure base’ for social workers and their managers is stressed if they are to provide the same for their clients.

Depressive position, paranoid-schizoid position, death instinct, group therapy, narcissistic organization, projective processes,

This paper explores the structure of groups and gangs and looks at the states of mind of the individuals within these different constellations from a descriptive and theoretical point of view. The terms ‘group’ and ‘gang’ are defined in specific ways as related to Klein's description of the depressive position, on the one hand, and the paranoid-schizoid position, on the other. The elaboration of these concepts by post-Kleinian writers, particularly Rosenfeld, is also examined. Drawing on examples from society, Philip Larkin's poem Aubade, William Golding's novel Lord of the Flies and clinical work with groups of children, the paper considers how and why ‘grouping’ and ‘ganging’ occur and what factors determine a move from one state of mind to another.

Trauma; play; autism; language development.

This paper will describe work in progress with a boy who was 3-4 years old at the time of referral. At this time he had no speech and there were a number of marked autistic features in his presentation, although no formal diagnosis had been made. He had suffered the trauma of a life-threatening illness requiring major medical interventions at the age of 5 months and again at 18 months, which may have been the precipitating factor for his disturbance. He is from an intact family with an older sister and a younger brother and no apparent significant family pathology.

During the course of his treatment—which has now been ongoing for nearly three years—he has acquired a capacity for play and has become very talkative. Using extensive clinical material, the paper will explore the factors which may have contributed to his improvement, especially the modifications in technique introduced by the therapist in order to make contact with this little boy. Special attention will be given to the role of playfulness, as introduced by the therapist, with particular reference to the way in which this may facilitate the emergence and expression of aggressive feelings and phantasies. The links with the development of the capacity for speech will be explored.

There is hope, even if not for us, Kafka reportedly once remarked. This book, long and eagerly awaited, is about the vicissitudes of hope in a puzzling, perhaps bizarre, area of human experience: autism. It does not disappoint. For those readers who follow a classic organic/biological model in thinking about autism, however, its contents may well be shocking and alarming.

It challenges the widely held view that psychotherapy, and in particular psychoanalytic psychotherapy, has nothing to offer to children and adolescents suffering from autistic spectrum disorders. The authors describe the clinical work and research undertaken by the Autism Workshop at the Tavistock Clinic London, both by themselves and by colleagues, over the last fifteen years, to help children and adolescents with autism and their families using psychoanalytic methods. The book is a sample of the experience gleaned from the workshop setting (Rustin, 1991).

The whole process has clearly been a major undertaking: the organization of the setting, the gathering of interested staff and students, the assessment of each individual family and child, the individual and group supervision, and the formulation of ideas, clinical, technical and theoretical. All these tasks are in service of the aim of considering how far psychoanalytical thinking and treatment can give meaning to the bizarre, fragmented and rigid behaviour of autistic children (p. 24).

The amount of effort, of course, must be reviewed in relation to the enormity of the assumptions and claims for the work. These are, first, that psychoanalytic psychotherapy and, in particular, the use of the countertransference as an important tool can effect a ‘major reversal of the [autistic] process’ in some children, and significantly improve the quality of life for other children and their families.

The aim of the work is to seek understanding as meaning for parents, family and child where there has been chaos, fragmentation and no-feeling (in the child) and despair (in the parents and family). But, they suggest, one of the limiting factors will be the personality of each child.

This book, which the editor describes as an international Festschrift, will be an enormous pleasure to all those who over the years have come into contact with Ann Alvarez and her work. To have what amounts to a companion edition to her first book Live Company (1992), now in its fourth edition, will also be a delight to many, and, to remind us of the poise and freshness of that book the present editor, Judith Edwards, has included as a foreword the original review by Victoria Hamilton from the Journal of Child Psychotherapy (1994, 20(1)). Another ‘echo’ of Live Company has also been cleverly worked into the front cover of the new book.

The work of Alvarez forms part of the widening (and deepening) scope of indications for child psychotherapy at the Tavistock Clinic since the 1960s when children with severe ego impairment (autism) were brought into analytic treatment. As this book illustrates, her work with psychotic, borderline and autistic children not only carries forward this tradition but has shaped its evolution. Today there is a growing curiosity in, study of and respect for contemporary Kleinian work with children and the vitalizing effects of Alvarez's contributions have been a potent stimulus for this interest. With her inventive use of Kleinian technique and her interest in theoretical debates, all communicated though a lucid writing style and a spry personal presence, her teaching and writings have allowed students and colleagues alike to cross many borders - between countries, between different disciplines, between different theoretical traditions within child psychotherapy itself. Writers from three different continents have contributed to this book and the editor has divided their contributions into two broad sections, covering theoretical and clinical contributions.

Mainly theory

Neil Altman begins by exploring the points of correspondence between Alvarez's technical ideas and the self-psychology and intersubjectivist approaches in North America. He describes Alvarez's technique as her way of presenting herself as a ‘real’ object and his interest is in demonstrating the therapeutic benefits of a balance struck between the therapist as a ‘real’ object and as a transference object which is interpreted. Altman highlights the debate in the USA between Kohut and Kernberg about whether idealization is developmental or defensive and he salutes Alvarez for rehabilitating the developmental aspects of idealization in Kleinian thinking. He also appreciates the application of projective identification to internal as well as external objects, though curiously he sees this as a recent development.
